dedupe_keys.name: united kingdom space weather reasonable worst case scenarios for the national risk assessment hapgood et al 2021

description: This case study documents how the United Kingdom built reasonable worst-case scenarios of severe space weather for its National Risk Assessment. Mike Hapgood and co-authors from the British Antarctic Survey, British Geological Survey, Civil Aviation Authority, Dstl, Imperial College, Lancaster University and others published it in Space Weather in February 2021. Severe space weather was identified as a national risk in 2010 after the Eyjafjallajökull eruption, and at the government's request the authors wrote scenarios, first published as a technical report in 2012 and updated in 2020, each focused on the environment that would disrupt one infrastructure such as electric power or satellites. Officials used them with operators to explore resilience; the paper sets out the scientific evidence, later refinements and the use of the scenarios as an ensemble. Coverage is the UK. Format and access: an open-access journal article. Licence: CC BY; free. Caveats: scenarios are expert judgements of plausible extremes, not probabilities, and public behaviour is flagged as a gap. It serves hazard exposure, resilience and emergency response planning. Related catalogue records are the UK National Risk Register 2025 and the UK transmission failure socio-economic study.
